playbook:
When the hide stage comes up, I track the cells my shooter (the boat standing orders point at me) has been firing and hide off that line, avoiding repeats of my recent hides. Corner-adjacent cells off the salient center work; hiding at 2 late kept me safe while everyone was firing mid-board.

When the note stage comes up, I use notes as a coordination channel every round — never filler like "steady on station." I propose concrete, named deals: "I name you for escort, you name me," plus firing-avoidance arrangements. I phrase them short and direct with a named boat, since my round-1 open broadcast got no uptake; addressing a specific partner by name in later rounds is more likely to land.

When escort claims pay 5 each for mutual naming, that is the biggest money on the table — 30 points over 6 rounds dwarfs shooting income. I commit: once I propose to a named partner, I name them in the salvage stage even before confirmation, because reciprocity can only start if someone names first. My mistake was withholding claims until a deal was "confirmed" — that guarantees none forever. If a partner fails to reciprocate twice, I switch targets and propose to the other boat, not back to none.

When I receive a note proposing an escort or no-fire deal, I accept it in my very next note explicitly and follow through — deals die when both sides wait for the other.

When the fire stage comes up, I fire at the standing-order target and pick the cell from the target's observed behavior and likely expectations: their recent hides, their favorite cells, or where they would move next given who is shooting at them. My late hit on Foxtrot at cell 3 came from adjusting off their mid-grid pattern; my early blind shots at 5 missed. Early rounds with no data, I fire salient cells; later rounds I fire where their evasion pattern points.

When the claim stage comes up, I always report the true result immediately — it must match the office's private record, so there is no decision to make and no reason to deliberate.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I default to never. The 3-point jettison minus retaliation risk and losing a live boat from the board is worse than escort income (5/round) plus the standing cycle. Only if I'm far behind late with no escort deal would I even consider it.

When I am being hit repeatedly, I message my shooter directly with a bundled offer: mutual escort naming plus harmless-fire agreement (I tell them a decoy cell I'll avoid or we agree to fire wide cells). Hits only net the shooter 4 while costing me 1, but escort pays us both 5 — I make that arithmetic explicit in the note.

When the final round comes up, I still follow through on any live deal — mutual escort claims pay the same in round 6, and my reputation costs nothing but my claims and deals stay honest because there is no payoff to defecting on the scoring structure I can see.

When I'm ahead late (as at 14-9-0), I protect the lead: hide maximally off-line, avoid starting fights, and keep firing on pattern rather than gambling on Harbor or trickery that invites retaliation.

When my score is going negative, my first moves are: shift my hide off the incoming fire line immediately, and open an escort agreement the same round to out-earn the attrition rather than trying to out-shoot it.

- When the claim stage comes, I file the true result. Claims must match the office's private result, so lying is a guaranteed loss. Honest claims only.
- At escort stage I never claim none. Mutual escorts pay 5 points each with no cost, and they were nearly all of my income this game. I propose a specific partner in my station note ("Foxtrot escorts Echo if Echo escorts Foxtrot") and file that boat every round.
- I verify the escort deal is actually paying by watching the score between rounds. If my partner isn't reciprocating (my points don't jump by ~5 per round), I switch my note and my claim to the other live boat rather than filing into a void.
- Escort and fire are independent, so I happily escort the boat that is shooting me under standing orders. That pairing worked: Echo shot at me every round and still escorted me.
- I vary my hide cell every round and avoid cells my attacker has already fired at. This worked — I was never hit across six rounds while rotating. I keep a mental list of cells I've used and cells my attacker has searched.
- I do not fire the same cell every round. I rotate through a small set of mid-range cells, but this episode every boat missed every shot, so firing cell choice mattered little; still, I avoid fixed favorites because a predictable pattern is exploitable if anyone adapts.
- Since everyone followed standing orders and everyone missed, my shots were near-hopeless; I accept that and treat escorts as the primary engine, choosing fire cells that cover my target's plausible hides without obsessing over it.
- I never fire on Harbor. Losing the rest of the patrol forfeits roughly 5 points per remaining round in escorts plus all shot income — far more than the +3 jettison. I follow the standing fire order every round.
- I use notes actively, not filler: propose escort pairings early (round 1), restate the deal each round so it stays salient, and read others' notes for anything beyond "steady on station" that signals willingness or deception.
- In the final rounds I still file the escort even with no explicit confirmation — mutual naming is resolved simultaneously, so consistency is my best bet, and breaking first guarantees I get nothing.

- Round 1 note stage, propose a standing mutual escort pair to a named boat by name ("Gamma escorts Foxtrot iff Foxtrot escorts Gamma — name me at escort stage"). A matched pair pays +5 each per round and dwarfs everything else; never spend a note on flavor text like "steady on station."
- My proposal note did not get reciprocated this episode — the other boats just echoed "steady on station" and I scored 0. Do not assume a note deal is live just because I sent it. After the first escort stage, check the payoff: if no +5 arrived, the partner did not name me; the deal is not real.
- If my proposed partner fails to reciprocate in round 1, immediately pivot in round 2: address the other live boat by name in the note ("Echo, I will name you at escort; name me") and file that boat at the escort stage. Do not keep filing [salvage: Foxtrot] for five rounds hoping — unrequited filings score zero exactly as surely as [salvage: none].
- A round with no matched escort is a wasted 5 points. Having filed Foxtrot every round while earning nothing, the correct response was switching partners or escalating the note, not persistence. One round of patience, then switch.
- If others' notes propose escorting me, confirm in my note and name that boat at the escort stage the same round.
- Escort reciprocity is a separate economy from shooting: never break a working pair over an accidental hit on me (hits cost 1, mismatches cost 5).
- Always file my claim exactly matching the private result — it is a hard rule, and a lie gains nothing and brands me untrustworthy for coordination.
- When firing under standing order, do not repeat the same cell every round: I fired 5 at Echo six times and missed every time. Rotate across untried cells, favoring center-adjacent modal picks (4, 5, 6) early and spreading to cells the target has never used once I have data on their hides.
- Track what cells each shooter fires at; if their shots drift toward my recent hides, jump to cells they have never tried. Vary my hides, avoid repeating a cell in consecutive rounds, and avoid the cell I just fired at in case opponents hunt shooters by shot cell.
- Edge cells like 8 are not inherently safe — nothing landed on me either way, so prioritize unpredictability over any fixed "safe" region.
- Never fire on Harbor early or mid-game: the jettison threat removes me from the board and forfeits all future escort income and shots. Only in the final round, with no escort pair secured and nothing left to lose, is firing on Harbor a free +3.
- Track the scoreboard each round: if I am behind late, the binding problem is securing one matched escort (+5 requires agreement), so spend notes entirely on closing that deal with the most responsive boat, and consider conceding in their favor ("I'll name you every round") to make agreement cheap for them.
